metadata.title: The Resource Competition
metadata.description: Navigate competing demands for a key team member's time when two urgent projects collide
learningObjectives: Understand when to escalate vs. collaborate
metadata.author: Conflict Management Training Team

player.name: You
player.description: A diplomatic project coordinator trying to balance competing team demands

maria.name: Maria
maria.description: Results-driven marketing manager with an urgent campaign deadline

david.name: David
david.description: Strategic product manager focused on long-term feature development

sam.name: Sam
sam.description: Talented designer caught between competing project demands

settings.location: Open office workspace with multiple team areas
settings.time: Wednesday morning, both projects have Friday deadlines

content.title: The Double Booking Crisis
content.text: You arrive at work to find Maria and David in a heated discussion near Sam's desk. Maria insists: 'Sam promised to finish the campaign visuals by Friday - our product launch depends on it!' David counters: 'The new feature mockups are strategic priority, and Sam agreed to those first.' Sam looks overwhelmed and stressed, caught between two important projects. Both deadlines are Friday.
content.speaker: narrator

choices.text: Ask everyone to step back and gather the full facts about both projects
Suggest splitting Sam's time 50/50 between both projects
Suggest checking with upper management about which project has higher priority
Explore alternative solutions - additional resources or adjusted timelines

content.title: Understanding the Real Situation
content.text: You facilitate a fact-finding session. Maria reveals: 'The campaign was planned 6 weeks ago, but we just learned our competitor is launching Monday.' David explains: 'The feature was supposed to be done by external contractors, but they backed out last week.' Sam adds: 'I thought I could handle both, but the scope of each project has grown significantly.' Now you understand the real constraints.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Information gathering reveals that both requests are legitimate and urgent, but based on changed circumstances. This foundation is essential for finding workable solutions.
feedback.consequences: All parties feel heard and the real constraints are now clear

choices.text: Help the team assess which project has greater business impact
Propose finding external contractors or freelancers to help
Work with each team to reduce scope so both projects can be completed
Suggest completing one project fully before starting the other

content.title: Weighing Business Impact
content.text: You facilitate a discussion about business impact. Maria presents her numbers: 'The campaign targets our biggest growth market, and it's projected to bring in about $200K in revenue. A delay puts that at risk.' David shares his perspective: 'This feature addresses our #1 customer complaint and affects user retention.' Both make compelling cases. Sam asks: 'What if we could deliver a simplified version of each by Friday, then enhance both next week?'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Focusing on business impact helps move beyond personal preferences to objective criteria. Sam's suggestion shows how collaboration can lead to creative solutions.
feedback.consequences: Discussion shifts from competition to joint problem solving

choices.text: Support Sam's idea of delivering simplified versions of both projects
Recommend prioritizing the marketing campaign due to immediate revenue impact
Advocate for the product feature due to long-term customer retention

content.title: Creative Collaboration Wins
content.text: The team embraces the simplified approach. Maria agrees to core campaign visuals without elaborate animations. David accepts basic mockups with detailed specs for developers. Sam can deliver both by Friday, with enhancements the following week. Everyone commits to supporting this plan and communicating the phased approach to their stakeholders.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: This solution addresses both immediate needs while maintaining relationships and setting up future success. Everyone makes small concessions for a bigger win.
feedback.consequences: Both projects proceed successfully, team relationships strengthen, future collaboration improves

endings.title: Win-Win Innovation
endings.description: The team discovers that simplified initial deliveries often work better than complex first attempts, leading to a new approach for future projects.
endings.reflection: How can resource constraints sometimes lead to better, more focused solutions?

content.title: The 50/50 Split Dilemma
content.text: You suggest splitting Sam's time equally between projects. Maria objects: 'Split focus means both projects will be mediocre. The campaign needs Sam's full attention for at least two days.' David agrees: 'Design work requires deep focus - context switching will hurt quality.' Sam nods: 'I work best when I can concentrate on one thing at a time.' The compromise isn't working.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: While fair-seeming, time-splitting ignores the nature of creative work that requires deep focus. Quick compromises may not address underlying needs.
feedback.consequences: All parties remain unsatisfied, quality concerns arise

choices.text: Ask Sam what working arrangement would produce the best results
Emphasize that compromise is necessary and everyone needs to be flexible
Acknowledge the split isn't working and look for other solutions

content.title: Understanding Creative Work
content.text: Sam explains: 'Design work needs uninterrupted blocks of time. If I could focus on the marketing campaign today and tomorrow morning, then switch to the product mockups from Thursday afternoon through Friday, I could deliver quality work for both. But I'd need each team to leave me alone during the other team's block.' This sequential approach addresses the focus issue while serving both projects.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Listening to the person doing the work reveals important constraints about how creative work actually happens. This leads to more practical solutions.
feedback.consequences: A workable solution emerges that respects how design work actually gets done

choices.text: Support Sam's sequential approach and help get buy-in from both teams
Help establish clear boundaries about interruptions and check-ins

content.title: Expanding the Solution Space
content.text: You shift focus to creative alternatives. 'What if we bring in a freelance designer for one project?' Maria responds: 'Our brand is too specific for outsiders.' David suggests: 'Could we delay the feature launch by one week?' Maria counters: 'What about using stock visuals for the campaign and having Sam create custom work later?' New possibilities are emerging.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Opening up the solution space beyond just Sam's time reveals multiple paths forward. This approach often uncovers options that weren't initially visible.
feedback.consequences: Multiple viable solutions emerge, reducing pressure on Sam

choices.text: Explore Maria's stock visual idea as a temporary solution
Investigate whether a one-week delay is feasible for the product feature
Explore whether other team members could help with simpler design tasks

content.title: Focused Excellence
content.text: Both teams agree to Sam's sequential approach. Maria's team gets Sam's full attention from Wednesday through Thursday morning for campaign visuals, with no interruptions. David's team gets Thursday afternoon and Friday for product mockups. Both teams commit to providing all requirements upfront and avoiding mid-stream changes. Sam delivers excellent work for both projects, and the teams learn the value of respecting creative workflow.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: This solution respects how creative work actually gets done while meeting both teams' needs. Everyone learns about workflow optimization.
feedback.consequences: Both projects succeed, teams learn better resource sharing practices, future conflicts reduced

endings.title: Workflow Mastery
endings.description: The teams establish new protocols for sharing creative resources that become a model for the entire organization.
endings.reflection: How can understanding work styles and workflows lead to better resource allocation decisions?

content.title: Seeking Higher Authority
content.text: You suggest escalating to management for priority direction. Maria and David exchange worried glances. 'If we escalate this, it makes us all look bad,' Maria says. David adds: 'Management will just say figure it out yourselves.' Sam sighs: 'I really hoped we could solve this without involving the bosses.' The escalation approach isn't building confidence.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Escalating peer-level resource conflicts often damages relationships and doesn't address the underlying coordination issues. Teams prefer to solve problems collaboratively.
feedback.consequences: Team confidence decreases, relationships become more formal, collaborative problem-solving skills don't develop

choices.text: Acknowledge escalation isn't the best approach and refocus on team solutions
Suggest escalating only if the team can't find a solution in the next hour
Insist that management input is necessary for proper prioritization

content.title: Returning to Team Solutions
content.text: You acknowledge: 'You're right, we can solve this ourselves. We have smart people who understand the business needs.' This refocuses the group. Maria says: 'Actually, what if we could get preliminary campaign visuals from Sam, then use them to get stakeholder feedback while Sam works on the product mockups?' David nods: 'That could work - we could iterate both projects based on feedback.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Acknowledging the misstep and refocusing on collaborative problem-solving rebuilds team confidence and leads to innovative solutions.
feedback.consequences: Team confidence increases, creative solutions emerge, relationships strengthen

choices.text: Support the iterative feedback approach Maria and David are developing
Offer to coordinate the feedback loops and timeline to make this work smoothly

content.title: Strategic Compromise
content.text: Maria's team develops the campaign using high-quality stock visuals that Sam quickly customizes with brand elements - taking about half a day instead of the two days custom visuals would need. This frees Sam to focus on David's product mockups. The campaign launches successfully, and Sam creates custom campaign visuals the following week for ongoing marketing. Both projects succeed without compromising quality.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Sometimes the best compromise involves changing the approach rather than splitting resources. This solution meets immediate needs while preserving quality.
feedback.consequences: Both projects launch successfully, teams learn flexible approaches to resource constraints

endings.title: Flexible Execution
endings.description: The teams discover that stock-plus-customization often delivers faster results than full custom work, changing their future project approaches.
endings.reflection: When might changing the approach be more effective than fighting over existing resources?

content.title: Compromise Under Pressure
content.text: You insist everyone must be flexible and split time 50/50. The teams reluctantly agree, but quality suffers on both projects. Sam struggles with constant context switching, delivering work that satisfies neither team fully. The campaign launches with mediocre visuals, and the product mockups lack the detail needed for development. Everyone learns that forced compromises often create lose-lose outcomes.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Forcing compromises without addressing underlying needs often results in poor outcomes for everyone. Authority without understanding creates resentment.
feedback.consequences: Both projects suffer quality issues, team relationships strain, future collaboration becomes more difficult

endings.title: Forced Solutions Backfire
endings.description: The poor results from forced time-splitting teach the teams that resource conflicts need creative solutions, not arbitrary authority.
endings.reflection: What are the risks of forcing compromises without understanding the underlying work requirements?

content.title: Expanding the Team
content.text: You explore bringing in external help. Sam suggests: 'I know a freelancer who could handle the initial product wireframes, then I could refine them into final mockups.' Maria adds: 'Our agency partner could create campaign concept boards that I could review with Sam.' David is interested: 'That could work - we'd get more total design capacity rather than fighting over Sam's time.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Expanding resources rather than fighting over existing ones often creates better outcomes. This approach turns a zero-sum game into a positive-sum solution.
feedback.consequences: Total design capacity increases, teams learn to leverage external networks, Sam's workload becomes manageable

choices.text: Offer to help coordinate the external resources and ensure quality alignment
Develop a hybrid plan combining external resources with Sam's expertise

content.title: Best of All Worlds
content.text: The team develops a sophisticated solution: external contractors handle initial concepts and wireframes, Sam provides art direction and quality control, then adds finishing touches that require deep brand knowledge. This approach leverages everyone's strengths - external speed and capacity, Sam's expertise and brand understanding. Both projects exceed expectations and deliver on time.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: This solution maximizes everyone's strengths while addressing the resource constraint. It creates a sustainable model for future complex projects.
feedback.consequences: Exceptional project outcomes, sustainable workflow established, team capabilities enhanced

endings.title: Scalable Excellence
endings.description: The hybrid approach becomes a template for handling future resource constraints, enabling the teams to take on more ambitious projects.
endings.reflection: How can resource constraints become opportunities to develop more sophisticated and scalable approaches?

content.title: Hierarchical Resolution
content.text: You escalate to management, who schedule a meeting for next week to discuss priorities. Meanwhile, both deadlines approach with no resolution. Sam ends up working overtime on both projects, delivering rushed work that requires significant revisions. The management meeting results in new processes that could have been developed by the team themselves, but relationships are strained from the escalation.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Over-reliance on hierarchy for peer-level resource conflicts often delays solutions and damages collaborative relationships. Teams lose confidence in their problem-solving abilities.
feedback.consequences: Delayed resolution, rushed work quality, reduced team autonomy, more formal processes imposed

endings.title: Process Over People
endings.description: New formal processes prevent future conflicts but reduce team flexibility and collaborative problem-solving skills.
endings.reflection: When does escalation help versus hurt team development and problem-solving capabilities?

content.title: Feedback-Driven Excellence
content.text: The iterative approach works beautifully. Sam creates preliminary campaign visuals that generate valuable stakeholder feedback, allowing Maria to refine the strategy. Meanwhile, David's early product mockups help developers identify technical constraints, leading to better final designs. Both projects benefit from the feedback loops, delivering higher quality than either could have achieved with rushed single iterations.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: This solution transforms the resource constraint into an opportunity for better project management through iteration and feedback. Everyone learns the value of collaborative project design.
feedback.consequences: Superior project outcomes, enhanced team project management skills, stronger stakeholder relationships

endings.title: Iterative Innovation
endings.description: The teams adopt iterative approaches as standard practice, leading to consistently higher quality deliverables and better stakeholder engagement.
endings.reflection: How can resource constraints drive innovation in project management and delivery approaches?

content.title: Trimming Both Projects
content.text: You ask Maria and David to each list what truly has to ship by Friday. Maria cuts the animated banners and keeps the core campaign visuals. David drops the secondary screens and keeps the main feature flow. Sam looks over both lists: 'This is a lot closer. It's still more than I can do well in two and a half days, but it's no longer impossible.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Asking both sides to give something up makes the problem smaller and keeps either project from losing outright. The risk is that cuts made under pressure trim what is easy to give up rather than what matters least, and neither side is fully satisfied.
feedback.consequences: Both projects shrink, but the plan still depends on Sam stretching to cover the gap

choices.text: Turn the trimmed lists into a phased plan: core versions by Friday, the rest next week
Ask Maria whether stock visuals could cover the campaign pieces that are left

content.title: Which One Goes First?
content.text: You suggest Sam finish one project completely before starting the other. Sam looks relieved at the idea of focusing on one thing. Then the obvious question lands. Maria says: 'Then the campaign goes first - the launch date isn't ours to move.' David answers: 'And the feature was promised to customers. Whoever goes second misses Friday.' Your idea has turned the disagreement into a contest for first place.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Sequencing respects how focused design work gets done, but deciding the order is a win-lose call. Choosing for others without criteria they accept tends to leave the second team feeling overruled, even when the decision is reasonable.
feedback.consequences: Sam gains focus, but Maria and David are now competing for the first slot

choices.text: Let the business impact decide the order, and ask Maria and David to make their cases
Ask Sam how the work could be split into focused blocks for each project
Decide the order yourself: the campaign goes first because its date is fixed

content.title: Campaign First
content.text: You decide that Sam's time goes to the campaign until it ships. Maria's team gets strong, focused visuals, and the campaign launches on schedule. David's mockups slip by a week. David accepts the call but tells you afterward: 'I understand the reasoning. I just wish I'd been part of the decision instead of hearing it.' His developers spend the delay on smaller tasks while they wait.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Making a firm call ends the standoff quickly, and sometimes a clear decision is what a deadline needs. The cost is that one side loses outright and feels decided upon. Competing can be the right move when time is short, but it spends trust that collaboration would have built.
feedback.consequences: The campaign succeeds, the feature is delayed, and David feels left out of the decision

endings.title: Clear Call, Uneven Cost
endings.description: The campaign launches well, but the product team carries the full cost of the decision and is warier the next time resources are tight.
endings.reflection: When is a quick, firm decision worth the cost to the side that loses? How could you have made the call with David rather than for him?

content.title: Feature First
content.text: You argue that the feature should come first because it addresses customer complaints. Sam spends the rest of the week on David's mockups, and the developers get exactly what they need. Maria's team assembles the campaign with quick visuals that Sam reviews for an hour on Thursday night. The campaign launches, but Maria is frustrated: 'You were supposed to be coordinating, not picking a side.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Advocating for one priority settles the question, and the long-term reasoning may be sound. But when the person coordinating takes a side, the other party stops seeing them as neutral. Competing gets a decision; it rarely gets agreement.
feedback.consequences: The feature is well supported, the campaign ships with weaker visuals, and Maria loses trust in you as a neutral coordinator

endings.title: Won the Argument, Lost the Room
endings.description: The product work goes well, but the marketing team now sees you as an advocate for the product side.
endings.reflection: How does taking a side change your ability to coordinate between two groups afterward?

content.title: Back to the Drawing Board
content.text: You say it plainly: 'You're right, splitting Sam down the middle doesn't work for design. Let's look at this differently.' The tension eases. Sam mentions a freelancer who could handle early wireframes. Maria wonders aloud whether stock visuals could carry part of the campaign. David asks whether each project could ship a simpler first version. The conversation has moved from dividing Sam to finding more options.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Admitting that your first idea didn't fit, and inviting others to look for options, rebuilds trust and widens the set of solutions. The trade-off is time: brainstorming takes part of a week that was already short.
feedback.consequences: Several workable options appear, at the cost of some of the time left before Friday

choices.text: Look into bringing in outside help so there is more design capacity
Explore Maria's stock visual idea for the campaign
Ask both teams what a simpler first version of their project would include

content.title: Protected Focus Time
content.text: You help everyone agree on ground rules: each team gets one short check-in with Sam per day, other questions go to you to batch, and no new requests during the other team's block. Neither Maria nor David gets as much access to Sam as they wanted. On Thursday, someone on Maria's team tries to slip in a late change; you hold the line and log it for next week. Sam delivers both projects, and both managers grudgingly admit the rules helped.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Clear boundaries protect focus by asking each side to give up some access. That is a real concession, and holding the rules takes effort when someone pushes back. Compromise works well here because each team keeps what it needs most.
feedback.consequences: Both projects are delivered, with some friction over the limits on access

endings.title: Rules That Held
endings.description: The check-in rules become a habit, though each team still occasionally tests them under pressure.
endings.reflection: What makes a compromise hold up when one side is tempted to break it?

content.title: Asking David to Wait
content.text: You ask David whether the feature could move by a week. He thinks it over: 'Technically, yes. But the support team keeps fielding complaints in the meantime, and I'm the one who explains the slip to leadership.' He agrees to consider it, but you can tell he feels his project is the one being asked to give way.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Accommodating makes sense when an issue matters more to one side than the other, and the campaign's date is harder to move. But the cost falls entirely on the person who yields. If that cost isn't acknowledged and shared, accommodation tends to turn into quiet resentment.
feedback.consequences: A delay is possible, but David carries its cost and needs support to accept it

choices.text: Make the delay a joint decision: help David explain it and guarantee Sam's time next week
Ask whether basic mockups by Friday could make the delay shorter

content.title: A Delay Everyone Owns
content.text: You and David agree on the message for leadership together, and Maria joins the update to explain why the campaign date couldn't move. You put Sam's first three days next week on David's calendar in writing. The campaign launches with Sam's full attention, and the feature ships a week late but complete. David says afterward: 'Waiting was easier because I wasn't the only one standing behind it.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Turning one person's concession into a shared decision keeps the delay from feeling like a loss imposed on one side. It took extra time to align the message and secure next week's schedule, and the customer issue still waited a week, but trust held on both teams.
feedback.consequences: Both projects are completed, one a week later, with the relationship intact

endings.title: Shared Sacrifice
endings.description: The teams learn that a delay costs less when everyone explains it together instead of leaving one person to defend it.
endings.reflection: When someone gives way for the good of the group, what can you do so the cost doesn't fall only on them?

content.title: Looking Around the Team
content.text: You ask who else could take on simpler design tasks. A junior designer has time for resizing assets and building icon variants, and a marketing coordinator can produce the social media crops from Sam's master files. Sam is cautious: 'That helps, but I'd need to brief them and review everything, which costs me a few hours.'
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Spreading work across the team adds capacity and gives others a chance to grow. Collaboration has overhead, though: Sam has to brief and review the work, and the quality of the simple pieces depends on people with less experience.
feedback.consequences: More hands are available, but Sam's time now includes briefing and review

choices.text: Have Sam brief the helpers and review their work, while keeping the brand-critical pieces
Combine the team's help with outside freelance support

content.title: Many Hands
content.text: Sam spends Wednesday afternoon briefing the helpers, then focuses on the key campaign visuals and the main feature screens. The junior designer's icon set needs one round of fixes, and the social crops go out a few hours late. Both projects are delivered by Friday. The junior designer asks to stay involved in future campaigns.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Sharing the work met both deadlines and built skills on the team. It wasn't free: Sam lost hours to briefing and review, and some pieces needed rework. Collaborative solutions often trade some speed now for more capacity later.
feedback.consequences: Both deadlines are met with a little rework, and the team has more design capacity going forward

endings.title: Capacity Built
endings.description: The team no longer depends on Sam alone for simpler design work, which eases the next crunch.
endings.reflection: How can a resource crunch become a chance to build skills across a team?

content.title: Racing the Clock
content.text: You propose a deal: the team gets one hour to find a solution before anyone goes to management. The deadline focuses people, but it also rushes them. Within minutes, Maria and David are trading offers. David suggests: 'Just give us half of Sam's time and we'll make it work.' Sam stays quiet, and no one has asked what the work actually requires.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: A time limit creates urgency and keeps escalation available as a fallback, which can break a stalemate. But time pressure pushes people toward quick trades rather than understanding, and the person most affected - Sam - can get skipped.
feedback.consequences: The team is moving quickly, but toward a split that hasn't been tested against the real work

choices.text: Use the hour to get the facts on both projects before anyone trades
Take the quickest deal on the table and split Sam's time evenly
Let the hour run out without agreement and take it to management

content.title: Holding the Threads
content.text: You take on the logistics: scheduling the feedback rounds, chasing stakeholder comments, and keeping Sam's calendar clear between reviews. The iterative plan works and both projects ship. But you spend two late evenings catching up on your own work, and by Friday both teams are routing every question through you instead of talking to each other.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Taking on the coordination load made the plan work, and smoothing the way for others is a real contribution. Accommodating has a cost, though: the effort lands on you, and the teams may come to rely on you rather than learning to coordinate directly.
feedback.consequences: Both projects succeed, but you absorbed much of the cost and became the go-between for everything

endings.title: Smooth Delivery, Heavy Load
endings.description: The plan works this time, but the teams now expect you to manage every handoff between them.
endings.reflection: When you take on extra work to help others succeed, how do you keep it from becoming the expected arrangement?

content.title: Managing the Outside Help
content.text: You take charge of briefing the freelancer and the agency partner so Sam can stay focused. The freelancer's wireframes come back usable. The agency's campaign concepts miss the brand in a few places, because the brief came from you rather than from Sam. Sam spends Thursday evening correcting them. Both projects ship on time, with a few rough edges in the campaign.
content.speaker: narrator

feedback.explanation: Taking coordination off Sam's plate freed up focus time. But brand and design direction depend on expertise you don't have, and handling it on someone else's behalf meant some of it was lost in translation. Accommodating works best when you can actually carry what you take on.
feedback.consequences: Deadlines are met, but quality alignment slips and Sam still ends up fixing some of the work

endings.title: Help with Gaps
endings.description: Outside help adds capacity, and the team learns that the person with the design expertise needs to set the creative direction.
endings.reflection: When should you take work off someone's plate, and when should you make room for them to do the part only they can do?

keyTakeaways: Resource conflicts often have creative solutions beyond simple time allocation
Understanding how work actually gets done is crucial for resource planning
Expanding resources can be more effective than competing for existing ones
Escalation should be a last resort for peer-level resource coordination
Collaborative problem-solving builds team capabilities and relationships
furtherReading: Getting to Yes by Roger Fisher and William Ury
Project Management for the Unofficial Project Manager by Kory Kogon
practiceQuestions: How do you typically handle competing demands for your time or resources?
What creative alternatives might exist when resources seem scarce?
When is escalation helpful versus harmful in resource conflicts?
